kicker: The market it was born into
title: Everything was going clear
lede: Zima arrived at the height of a short fashion for transparent versions of familiar products, and at a moment when brewers were looking for something to sell to people who did not like beer.

blocks.title: The clear craze
blocks.body:
In March 1993 the Washington Post listed the clear products then on sale: Crystal Pepsi from PepsiCo, a clear Sensor deodorant from Gillette and a clear Ivory dishwashing liquid from Procter & Gamble, each betting that shoppers would read colourless as pure. The same report asked whether the idea would work for beer, and mentioned that Coors “is testing a clear malt beverage, called Zima in three markets.”[^25] Westword later added Tab Clear and a clear Amoco gasoline to the list, and noted that all of them had since vanished.[^22]

Coors drew one lesson from Miller’s experiment. Miller Clear had the word beer on the label and disappointed beer drinkers. Coors called its product a “clearmalt,” positioned it as neither beer nor wine cooler, and instructed stores not to shelve it beside the coolers.[^13] Miller Clear never left its test markets.[^25]

blocks.text: Zima just is. Why question it. Go with the flow.
blocks.who: zima.com, “What is Zima?”, as captured in October 1996[^33]

blocks.title: What it was
blocks.caption: Original illustration, not an official asset.
blocks.body: A malt beverage brewed like beer and then filtered until nothing of the beer was left but the alcohol. The brand’s website gave the strength as 4.6% by volume and the energy as 148 calories per 12 ounces.[^33]
